Earnings quality: follow the profit into cash

Read an earnings-to-cash bridge, test working capital and capital spending, and distinguish a temporary cash shortfall from a weak business model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

On this page

  1. Start with the claim you are trying to test
  2. Build a bridge from net income to operating cash
  3. Test the working-capital explanation
  4. Separate maintenance needs from expansion claims
  5. Audit adjustments before using an adjusted P/E
  6. Turn the evidence into a valuation decision
  7. Sources and scope
  8. Continue reading

The central idea

An attractive earnings multiple needs an explanation of how those earnings become cash available to owners.

01

Start with the claim you are trying to test

A company reports rising earnings, yet its cash balance is falling. That observation is a question to investigate. The business might be building inventory for signed orders, opening stores, repaying debt, or struggling to collect money from customers. Each explanation has a different implication for future earning power.

Our research approach is to write one testable sentence before building a valuation: “The company can convert its reported profit into cash after maintaining the assets required to earn it.” Then identify which disclosures would support or weaken that sentence. A low P/E alone cannot answer it.

The SEC financial-statement guide distinguishes income, cash flows, and the balance sheet. Read the statements together: profit measures a period, the balance sheet records resources and obligations at a date, and the cash-flow statement reconciles cash movements.

02

Build a bridge from net income to operating cash

Consider an invented manufacturer. Every amount below is in millions and covers the same financial year. The bridge uses an indirect cash-flow presentation. It simplifies the statement to expose the main drivers.

Worked example · same year, same reporting perimeter
ComponentCash-flow adjustment
Net income100
Depreciation and amortization+25
Stock-based compensation+10
Increase in receivables−30
Increase in inventory−20
Increase in payables+15
Operating cash flow100
Cash purchases of property and equipment−45
Simplified free cash flow55

Operating cash flow equals net income here, but the business still needs 45 of capital spending. The remaining 55 is a starting point for examining financing capacity. It has not yet paid dividends, repurchased shares, completed acquisitions, or met debt principal repayments.

The stock-compensation add-back deserves separate attention. It is noncash in this period, but new shares can dilute ownership. Treating the add-back as permanently free money while assuming an unchanged share count would make the owner-return model inconsistent.

03

Test the working-capital explanation

In this example, receivables and inventory absorb 50 while payables supply 15. Ask whether the 35 net cash use represents healthy expansion, deteriorating collections, or goods that may need discounting. Compare several periods and use consistent definitions.

Suppose revenue rises from 800 to 1,000 while year-end receivables rise from 80 to 150. Receivables increase from 10% to 15% of annual sales. That is a useful warning flag; it does not prove customers are failing to pay. Seasonality, acquisitions, payment terms, and the timing of large invoices can all change the ratio. Average balances and credit-sales data would improve the test.

Read the receivables aging, credit-loss allowance, inventory policy, and management discussion. Compare the explanation with later collections. A working-capital release can also flatter cash flow: collecting old invoices or running down inventory can produce strong cash in a year with weak new demand.

04

Separate maintenance needs from expansion claims

The 45 capital-spending figure is observable in our example. The split between maintenance and growth is an analytical judgment unless the company discloses a reliable breakdown. Calling all spending “growth investment” can overstate cash available for distribution.

Test a range. If maintaining productive capacity requires 25, cash after that requirement would be 75 before other claims. If it requires the full 45, the result is 55. Those are alternative assumptions, not two versions of reported free cash flow. Record the basis for the split rather than presenting your preferred answer as an accounting fact.

Also inspect leases, acquisitions, capitalized development, and supplier financing. The cash-flow classification can vary with the accounting framework and transaction. A consistent multi-year analysis should explain which outflows it includes and avoid comparing unlike definitions.

05

Audit adjustments before using an adjusted P/E

Management may exclude restructuring, acquisition costs, impairments, or compensation from an adjusted earnings measure. Start with the reconciliation and ask what economic activity produced each adjustment. Repeated exclusions need a reason to disappear from a future forecast.

The SEC’s non-GAAP interpretations discuss potentially misleading exclusions of recurring operating expenses and inconsistent adjustments. This is US disclosure guidance; it is not a substitute for the reporting rules that apply to a particular issuer.

For your model, preserve reported and adjusted results side by side. If reported EPS is 4.00 and adjusted EPS is 5.00, a price of 80 represents 20× reported earnings and 16× adjusted earnings. Neither denominator is automatically the right forecast anchor. Explain why an excluded cost will not recur or retain a realistic allowance for it.

06

Turn the evidence into a valuation decision

  1. Reconcile three to five years of net income, operating cash, capital spending, and share count.
  2. Identify temporary working-capital movements and test whether they later reverse.
  3. Document maintenance-spending assumptions and other contractual cash claims.
  4. Read adjusted-earnings reconciliations and identify exclusions that repeatedly return.
  5. Stress revenue, margins, collections, and funding together before selecting an earnings multiple.

A useful conclusion names both the evidence and the unresolved issue: “Cash conversion improved after collections normalized, but the maintenance-spending requirement remains uncertain.” That sentence tells the next researcher what to verify. It is more useful than a single quality score detached from the statements.

For banks and insurers, deposits, investments, regulatory capital, and financing are central to operations. Do not transfer this manufacturer’s free-cash-flow template mechanically to a financial institution. Use a framework suited to its business and capital constraints.
